Paris, October 1853.

From the notebook of François Arago, astronomer, Perpetual Secretary of the Academy of Sciences.

The weather this week has been fair, and I have been able to resume the measurements postponed since the spring. This morning I reviewed the accounts of the Observatory and signed the order for the new clock regulator. There is a letter from Leverrier still to answer, and the proofs of the memoir on terrestrial magnetism are late from the printer. Yesterday I said to my assistant:

"In the absence of anything better to do, I have had my boots mended, but the cost is considerable. If you have time this morning, you might give them another polish and have the stitching redone." I was wrong, however, to say that there was nothing better to do. A very important thing had come to my mind.

“Levasseur, if the earth were to fall down the sky it would not change the results of our measurements. But if the sky were to fall down, it would upset everything!”

He said, “Not everything, Monsieur.”

I said, “What do you mean?”

He said, “The Observatory.”

“I mean,” I said, “that the results of our work would be no longer valid.”

“You seem to have a new preoccupation.”

“It is the problem of the tides, monsieur. I have been reading the new paper from M. Cauchy.”

“Yes. He says that the tides are an example of a non-linear system.”

“He says the tide-producing forces are not additive.”

“The tide-producing forces are not additive.”

The weather was fair on the next day also, and I made the necessary calculations. I made out the accounts and sent them to the Comptroller of the Academy. There is still no word from Leverrier, and I have written again. I took my dinner and went to bed, but could not sleep.

He replied:

“I have been engaged at the Observatory for twenty-four hours, and I do not even know which day it is.”

“But how did you sleep?” I asked.

“I slept soundly, M. Arago.”

“And you did not dream about your work?”

“I dreamed, M. Arago.”

“Do you know, I believe we have a spy in our midst?”

“A spy, sir?”

“Yes. There is an observer at work in our garden, every day, in plain view.”

“In plain view, sir?”

“Yes. I see him as I look from my window, and he must see me. He is a very old man. He has been at it for years.”

The new observatory on the heights of Meudon will be a magnificent edifice, but I must not lose sight of the work that remains to be done in Paris.

I was working on the accounts when a knock sounded at the door. I answered, “Come in,” and saw a man about my own age, a bit taller and heavier, dressed in a fine blue suit.

“Good evening,” he said. “You are Dr. Arago?”

“Yes.”
